newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe to wait some more for crucial donor aid.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe to wait some more for crucial donor aid.

text.p: The World Bank commended Zimbabwe on Wednesday for efforts to curtail government expenditure, but said release of crucial balance of payments aid depended on further progress in cutting the budget deficit.

David Cook, the World Bank's representative in Zimbabwe, told a news conference the bank was also waiting for President Robert Mugabe's government to finalise a new five-year economic reform programme before making this decision.

"We're impressed by government efforts to make sure that the budget deficit goes down. We are impressed by what's going on. One needs to get the deficit down to a level that's sustainable and we're not yet there," he said at the end of annual aid talks.

"The budget deficit remains quite high. The problem has been made difficult to deal with by the increase in the civil servants wage bill," Cook added, referring to unbudgeted-for salary rises of more than 20 percent the government awarded last year to civil servants following a series of strikes.
The government has to raise an extra Z$3 billion (U.S.$269 million) to finance the salary increases and Cook said this was likely to widen the budget deficit.

He would not say how far off the deficit was likely to be from a target of 8.5 percent of gross domestic product set in the 1996/97 budget ending in June. Zimbabwe's Finance Minister Herbert Murerwa said last week the deficit was likely to exceed 11 percent.

The government has repeatedly missed key spending reduction targets since it embarked on World Bank and International Monetary Fund-backed economic reforms in 1991. This led to the two bodies withholding crucial balance of payments support in 1995.

"What happens in the next months and in the budget will be very important when determining the funds to be released," Barbara Kafka, World Bank director for Angola, Malawi and Zimbabwe, told Wednesday's news conference.
Other key Western donors say their supoport for Zimbabwe's next phase of economic reforms would depend on the government reaching an agreement with the World Bank and the IMF.

National Economic Planning Commission director Edgar Chigudu reaffirmed the government's commitment to cutting the budget deficit through improved tax collection, overhaul of the budget and expenditure control system and accelerating the privatisation of loss-making state firms.

The two-day meeting between the World Bank and Zimbabwe produced an agreement on a standard development aid programme aimed largely at reducing poverty in the southern African country which included support for projects in agricultural and social sectors as well as for infrastructural and community development.
